analysis.one_liner: Opens federal offshore waters to natural gas drilling and splits royalties with coastal states.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: introduced in September 2005 with 24 cosponsors from both parties, it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have wiped out every federal law and presidential order that keeps parts of the Outer Continental Shelf — federal waters off America's coasts — closed to natural gas drilling. It would have required the Interior Department to put up at least 75 percent of all unleased offshore acreage for drilling in each five-year leasing plan, created a new type of lease restricted to natural gas, and given coastal states 50 percent of the bonus bids and royalties from leases near their shores. The stated goal was to increase natural gas supply, which spiked in price after Hurricane Katrina in 2005.
analysis.who_benefits: Natural gas producers, who would gain access to vast new offshore acreage for exploration and drilling. Coastal state governments would gain a permanent 50 percent share of federal royalties from nearby gas leases. Consumers could see some benefit if new supply lowered heating and electricity prices, though that depends on market conditions and how quickly leases are developed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Offshore natural gas producers and coastal states

how_it_helps.text: It strips the force out of every federal provision that bars spending money on natural gas leasing and preleasing anywhere on the Outer Continental Shelf, opening the process to areas currently off-limits [S2] [S3].
It revokes all existing presidential withdrawals under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act with respect to natural gas, undoing protections that presidents had placed on offshore areas [S2] [S3].

It requires each five-year federal leasing program to offer for gas leasing at least 75 percent of the available unleased acreage in every Outer Continental Shelf planning area, a mandate that limits the Secretary's discretion to hold areas back [S2] [S3].

It gives coastal states 50 percent of bonus bid and royalty revenues from federal gas leases within their extended seaward boundaries, starting October 1, 2006, creating a direct financial stake for state governments in expanded drilling [S2] [S3].

It creates natural gas-only leases, a new lease type that restricts development to natural gas and associated condensate, which the sponsor framed as a compromise for areas where oil drilling is opposed [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coastal communities and the public bear the environmental risk of drilling in waters now protected by moratoria and presidential withdrawals: spills, pipeline and platform construction, and industrial activity near beaches that anchor tourism and fishing economies. The federal Treasury gives up half the bonus bids and royalties from leases near state boundaries, money that otherwise flows to the general fund. Any consumer price relief is uncertain and would come years after leasing begins.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coastal communities, tourism and fishing economies

drawbacks.text: The bill revokes all presidential withdrawals with respect to natural gas and lifts all leasing bans across the entire Outer Continental Shelf, including areas that have been under a bipartisan congressional and presidential moratorium since the early 1980s — it does not limit itself to areas with local support [S2] [S3].

The 75 percent leasing mandate forces the Interior Department to offer nearly all unleased acreage in every planning area, leaving the Secretary little room to exclude sensitive waters, a design that coastal-state opponents of offshore drilling strongly objected to when similar proposals were debated [S3].
The 50 percent royalty share with coastal states, paid out of federal gas leases, reduces revenue that otherwise goes to the U.S. Treasury and the general public [S2] [S3].

Even supporters of expanded drilling acknowledged in this era that new offshore supply takes many years to reach market, so the promised relief from high natural gas prices would be slow and uncertain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill promises long-term consumer benefit through more natural gas supply, but its costs fall on coastal communities that did not ask for drilling off their shores, and its royalty-sharing provision redirects public revenue to state governments. The mechanism most likely to move consumer prices — more offshore supply — is slow and speculative, while the environmental exposure is immediate and concentrated on specific places. The bill is also drafted broadly: rather than opening selected areas, it eliminates every existing protection at once, which is why it drew opposition even from members otherwise open to some drilling.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Natural Resources Committee and then its energy subcommittee, neither of which ever acted on it, and it expired when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. John Peterson of Pennsylvania introduced the Outer Continental Shelf Energy Relief Act on September 27, 2005, during a period of high natural gas prices following Hurricane Katrina [S1] [S5].

The bill attracted 24 cosponsors — 19 Republicans and 5 Democrats — but the House Committee on Resources referred it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources on October 12, 2005, and no further action was ever taken [S4] [S5].

The sponsor gave introductory remarks on the floor in early November 2005, but the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

The 109th Congress ultimately addressed offshore drilling differently: in 2006 it passed the Gulf of Mexico Energy Security Act, which opened a limited area of the eastern Gulf while preserving the longstanding moratorium on most of the Atlantic and Pacific coasts.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coastal communities and the tourism and fishing economies that depend on undisturbed waters are better off, because the drilling bans and presidential withdrawals the bill would have swept away remained in place. The U.S. Treasury also keeps 100 percent of royalties rather than ceding half to coastal states. Natural gas producers, meanwhile, did not get the expanded offshore access the bill promised.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including members from energy-producing states such as Oklahoma, Utah, Alaska, and Texas

against.what_they_did: Defended the decades-old moratorium on offshore drilling off most coasts; Congress instead passed the 2006 Gulf of Mexico Energy Security Act, which preserved the moratorium outside a limited eastern Gulf opening

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided: 19 of the 24 cosponsors were Republicans and 5 were Democrats, and the bill never advanced far enough for a vote that would have shown the full partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would hand producers access to vast new federal offshore acreage by wiping out leasing bans and presidential withdrawals and mandating that 75 percent of unleased acreage be offered. Consumers might see lower gas prices from added supply over time, but the environmental cost falls on coastal communities rather than the industry.

Drilling platforms, pipelines, and spill risk in waters now closed would threaten the beaches and fisheries these industries depend on. Their interest in keeping the waters closed runs alongside coastal residents' interest in the same thing.

The bill gives states 50 percent of bonus bids and royalties from gas leases within their expanded seaward boundaries, converting offshore drilling into a permanent state revenue stream. This share was designed to give coastal states a financial reason to accept drilling off their shores.

Half the bonus bids and royalties from leases near state boundaries would be diverted from the federal miscellaneous receipts account to state governments, reducing the public revenue from resources owned by all Americans.
